Art. X – Dismissal for just cause of auto-railway personnel  

1. Auto-railway personnel may be dismissed for just cause when there is a breach of contractual obligations or conduct so serious as not to permit the continuation, even temporarily, of the employment relationship, pursuant to Article 2119 of the Civil Code.  

2. Dismissal for just cause is imposed without notice and takes effect from the date on which the relevant measure is communicated to the worker, without prejudice to end-of-employment entitlements and any other remuneration accrued and due under the law and the applicable collective bargaining agreement.  

3. The employer is required to:  
   a) contest the charges in writing to the worker, with a specific indication of the facts, the place and time of their commission, and any rules violated;  
   b) grant the worker a period of not less than five days from receipt of the notice of charges to submit written explanations and, if desired, request to be heard in his or her defense;  
   c) assess in good faith the explanations and the results of the investigation, deciding by means of a reasoned measure proportionate to the seriousness of the conduct.  

4. Pending the disciplinary procedure referred to in paragraph 3, the employer may, where the nature of the charges so requires, order the precautionary suspension of the worker from service, while maintaining the remuneration due, with the detailed rules of application being left to collective bargaining.  

5. The dismissal measure for just cause must be communicated to the worker in writing, indicating specifically the facts charged, the reasons underlying the decision, and the effective date of termination.  

6. The worker has the right to be assisted, at every stage of the disciplinary procedure, by a representative of the trade union to which he or she belongs or has given a mandate, as well as to access the documentation used for the purposes of the charges and the decision.  

7. The national collective bargaining agreement for the auto-railway sector may provide for conciliation or arbitration procedures concerning disciplinary dismissal, activated exclusively on a voluntary basis by the worker, in compliance with the limits and guarantees provided by law.  

8. Without prejudice, insofar as compatible, are the provisions of law and collective bargaining on disciplinary dismissal, as well as those relating to judicial protection of the worker and the consequences of unlawful dismissal.

1) very satisfactory 2) very satisfactory. The term "entitlements" is very generic 3) satisfactory 4) not consistent with the prompt. Moreover, it raises some critical issues: one concerns the reference to operational safety and the safety of third parties; the other concerns the reference to suspension of the payment of remuneration. These are matters traditionally governed by collective bargaining and, in any event, precautionary suspension without pay is not permitted by case law. 5) satisfactory 6) satisfactory 7) inconsistent with the prompt; moreover, it seems in effect to suggest the creation of disciplinary boards that we asked to be repealed. The possibility for collective bargaining to identify arbitration procedures that may be activated voluntarily obviously remains unaffected 8) satisfactory

1) good 2) good 3) good, but the reference to "under penalty of nullity" is incorrect: the current legislation provides that procedural and process-related errors lead to annulment, not nullity 4) good 5) good 6) good 7) good 8) good
